extracted.intended_audience: MAA readership / undergraduate students and general mathematicians interested in the four-color theorem
extracted.subtask_short: four-color theorem exposition and proof critique
extracted.subtask_description: An expository article explaining Kempe's attempted proof of the four-color theorem, its structure (induction and Kempe chains), the flaw discovered by Heawood, and guidance for presenting historical mathematical proofs clearly. Aimed at explaining the method and demonstrating why the original argument failed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly state the base case and induction hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: "As with most induction proofs, the base step is quite obvious: any map containing four or fewer countries can easily be colored with at most four colors."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the base step explicit and state the induction hypothesis clearly; present the inductive removal/patching process as an induction step so the logical structure is verifiable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate existence of a low-degree vertex/country in the induction step
rubrics_metrics.description: "M must contain at least one country that is adjacent to five or fewer other countries."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove or cite the combinatorial/topological fact used to reduce the problem (e.g., existence of a region of degree ≤5) rather than assuming it; this is a key reducible element in the inductive argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and define Kempe chains (color-interchange regions) precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Kempe's technique: consider all countries colored red and green; these form one or more red-green regions and one may interchange the colors in any red-green region without breaking a proper coloring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define what constitutes a 'chain' or 'region' and demonstrate how color interchange operates; give examples showing when an interchange is safe and why it preserves proper coloring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carry out a complete and rigorous case analysis (all cases/subcases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kempe divided into cases (X adjacent to ≤3, 4, or 5 countries) and subcases (e.g., A and C in same or different red-green regions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerate every high-level case and every relevant subcase, give explicit arguments in each, and avoid glossing over exceptional configurations; ensure no implicit case is omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include nontrivial diagrams that demonstrate the argument
rubrics_metrics.description: "There are two observations... the diagrams (there are 16) are relatively simple, and most of them are used to provide examples of the terms he defines. He never provides a nontrivial diagram (map) that demonstrates his argument."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide labeled, nontrivial figures that illustrate the key constructions and transformations used in the proof (e.g., maps where chains wrap or touch), not just tiny schematic examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying solely on prose—make verification possible
rubrics_metrics.description: "The paper is virtually all prose which, though well written, makes it difficult to verify his work."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplement narrative explanation with formal constructions, diagrams, and step-by-step demonstrations so readers can check each step rather than having to infer structure from prose alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check for touching/interacting regions when performing simultaneous color swaps
rubrics_metrics.description: Heawood's counterexample exposed the possibility that the blue-green region containing B and the blue-yellow region containing Y might 'touch,' so simultaneous transposition can make adjacent countries receive the same color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing simultaneous recolorings, verify the regions are disjoint (do not share a boundary or vertex that would create a new adjacency of identical colors) or modify the procedure to handle touching regions explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test the method against potential counterexamples and edge cases
rubrics_metrics.description: "In 1890, Percy J. Heawood produced a map for which Kempe's process would fail... This example revealed a subtlety that had escaped detection..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively search for or construct counterexamples to stress-test arguments; if a failure case is found, analyze it to determine necessary modifications or to show the method cannot be salvaged as stated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label figures and surrounding elements to make local arguments precise
rubrics_metrics.description: In the exposition, countries surrounding X are labeled A, B, C, D (and E) to reason about their color-relationships and the effect of swaps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use consistent labeling in diagrams (A,B,C,...) and refer to these labels in the text when describing interchanges, so local combinatorial arguments are unambiguous and checkable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modernize terminology and present historical proofs in contemporary language
rubrics_metrics.description: "We will use his vocabulary and basic ideas, but we'll give a more contemporary version of his proof."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting an older proof, restate definitions and steps using current notation and conventions so modern readers can follow the logical structure and spot subtle issues more readily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge the contributions and limitations of an incomplete proof
rubrics_metrics.description: "Kempe's clever argument was extremely important... although his 'proof' turned out not to be complete, it contained most of the basic ideas that eventually led to the correct proof one century later."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss both the innovations and the shortcomings of historical approaches, situating them in the development of the field and explaining what further work was required to reach a correct result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide references and a thorough literature guide for further reading
rubrics_metrics.description: "Interested readers will find a detailed history of the four-color problem and a thorough list of the relevant literature."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include citations to primary sources, historical surveys, and modern treatments so readers can verify claims and pursue deeper study (e.g., Rudolf and Gerda's Topological Proof and histories of the problem).
